screens.prompt: In B10, count how many tickets have the status "Open".

hints.syntax: The criteria is text, so it needs quotes: =COUNTIF(B2:B9,"Open").
hints.func-countif: COUNTIF counts the rows that match a condition. COUNT cannot help you here: it counts numbers, and the status column is text.
hints.require-ref: The first argument has to be the status column itself, not the answer.
hints.value: One of the four Open rows is being missed. Check the range reaches the last ticket, and that "Open" is quoted exactly as it appears.
hints.error: #VALUE! here almost always means the criteria lost its quotes, so Excel tried to read Open as a cell name. Wrap the word in double quotes and keep the range as B2:B9.

reject.why: range stops one row short, so the last Open ticket is missed
COUNT counts non-empty cells, not ones that match
points at the ticket IDs instead of the status column
unquoted criteria is read as a name

screens.prompt: Turn filters on for the ticket table without leaving the keyboard.

hints.value: Filters toggle on the Data tab, at the end of the Sort & Filter group. The same keys switch them off again.

screens.prompt: Widen the Status column to fit its longest value, from the ribbon.

hints.value: Alt reaches the ribbon, H is the Home tab, O opens Format, and I is AutoFit Column Width.

docs.explain: COUNTIF walks the range and counts the cells that satisfy one condition. Eight tickets sit in B2:B9 with five different statuses, and exactly four of them read "Open", so COUNTIF(B2:B9,"Open") returns 4. Text conditions need quotation marks because the criteria is a string, while a numeric condition does not: COUNTIF(B2:B9,4) would count cells equal to the number four. The criteria also accepts comparisons and wildcards as text, so ">=5", "<>Closed" and "T-10*" are all legal conditions. COUNTIF is not case-sensitive for text, which surprises people who expect "open" and "Open" to count separately.

errors.text: The first argument is a single value instead of a range, or the criteria is missing its quotes.
COUNTIFF or COUNITF — a doubled letter is enough to lose the function.
A range that stops at B8 misses the last ticket, which is the most common reason a count is short by exactly one.

docs.atWork: Support queues, stock levels, failed payments: counting rows that match one condition is the most-used formula in any operations role, and the one most often done by scrolling and counting instead.
docs.outcome: Count the rows that meet a single condition.
